opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's increasingly true. Parameter count was always a bit of a proxy. It roughly told you how much memory a model has and how much compute you spend per token. For a long time those two things moved together, so it was a reasonable shorthand. But once you start decoupling them, the number on its own tells you a lot less.

That's actually a big part of what motivated our work on recurrent-depth models. The idea is that you can have a relatively small set of parameters, but you loop a block of layers many times in latent space before you emit a token. So the model can "think" longer on a hard problem without getting any bigger. At test time you can just turn up the number of iterations. Our 3.5-billion-parameter model, if you unroll it enough, is spending compute comparable to a much larger model. Then the question "how big is this model?" becomes ambiguous. Do you mean the weights on disk, or the effective depth it's using on a given problem?

And it's not just recurrence. Mixture-of-experts already broke the link between total parameters and active parameters. Chain-of-thought reasoning models break it in yet another way, because they spend compute by generating lots of tokens. So we have at least three different axes now: how much you store, how much you activate per token, and how many steps you take per answer.

I don't think parameter count is useless, though. It still matters a lot for memorization and knowledge. If you want a model to know a lot of facts about the world, you need storage, and you can't really loop your way into knowing trivia you never stored. But for reasoning-heavy tasks like math, code, or planning, it seems like a lot of the capability comes from compute rather than raw size. So I'd rather see comparisons that report something like FLOPs per answer, or performance as a function of test-time compute, alongside parameter count. That gives you a curve instead of a single number, and I think that's the more honest way to compare these systems going forward.

r001.rationale: It says a 3.5-billion-parameter model can spend compute comparable to a much larger model when unrolled, making model size ambiguous.

r002.rationale: It suggests reporting FLOPs per answer or performance versus test-time compute, but does not express pretraining compute as an equivalent conventional transformer size at a comparable token count.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the training node setup or whether it could train a conventional 32-billion-parameter transformer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's getting quite a bit less useful, and honestly I think it was always a somewhat flawed proxy that we got attached to because it was easy to measure. Parameter count was a decent stand-in for capability back when everyone was training roughly the same architecture with roughly the same recipe, and the main thing that varied was scale. Under those conditions, more parameters meant more capacity, and that tracked pretty well with what you could do with the model.

But the thing that parameter count actually measures is how much memory the model has, how much it can store. It was never really a measure of how much computation the model does. And what's changed is that we now have several different knobs for adding compute at inference time that don't touch the parameter count at all. The obvious one is chain-of-thought style reasoning, where the model generates a lot of tokens before it commits to an answer. But there's also the direction that I've been interested in, which is doing more computation in latent space, recurrently, so you reuse the same block of weights many times for a single token. In that setting you can have a model that is small by parameter count but that spends an arbitrary amount of compute on a hard problem, and that compute budget is really what determines how well it performs.

So if you have two models, one with 70 billion parameters that answers in one shot, and one with 8 billion that can iterate internally or externally for as long as it needs, the parameter counts tell you almost nothing about how they compare. They might be matched on an easy benchmark and wildly different on a hard one, in either direction depending on the task.

I think the more honest way to compare is something like total FLOPs spent per answer, or maybe a curve rather than a number, performance as a function of test-time compute. That's more annoying to report, and it makes comparisons less clean, but it reflects what's actually going on. Parameter count still matters for things like memory footprint and what hardware you can deploy on, so it's not useless, it's just become a deployment characteristic rather than a capability characteristic.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a 70-billion-parameter model answering in one shot with an 8-billion-parameter model that can compute iteratively, and says parameter counts tell little about their relative performance.

r002.rationale: It proposes comparing FLOPs spent per answer or performance versus test-time compute, but does not express a pretraining budget as the size of a conventional transformer trainable at a comparable token count.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the node setup used to train Geiping’s model or whether it could train a conventional 32-billion-parameter transformer.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, I think parameter count is becoming less useful as a standalone number. It still tells you something about the cost of storing a model and, depending on the architecture, the cost of running it. But it doesn’t tell you how much computation the model spends answering a particular question.

If you let the same model generate a much longer reasoning trace, or try several solutions and check them, you can get very different performance without changing the parameter count at all. So now you have another axis: how much compute are you willing to spend at inference time?

I think the more useful comparison is performance at a given computational budget. How good is the answer, how long did it take, and how much did it cost? Parameter count is still part of that picture, but it’s increasingly difficult to use it as a proxy for capability.

r001.rationale: The response says inference compute can vary for the same model, but does not identify a smaller model using more compute than a larger model.

r002.rationale: It does not propose expressing a pretraining compute budget as an equivalent conventional transformer size at a comparable token count.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the node setup used to train Geiping’s model or whether it could train a conventional 32-billion-parameter transformer.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I think parameter count is becoming less useful as a single number for comparing models. It still tells you something about the resources you need to store and run a model, but it doesn’t tell you how much computation the model spends answering a particular question.

If one model produces an answer immediately and another spends a long time generating intermediate reasoning, then comparing them just by parameter count misses a pretty substantial difference. A smaller model might get a better answer because you give it more time to work on the problem.

So I think we need to look at a few things together: the number of parameters, the training compute, and then the inference compute you spend per task. And for practical applications, you also care about latency and cost. How good an answer can you get within a particular budget? Parameter count is still part of that picture, but increasingly it’s not the whole picture.

r001.rationale: It says a smaller model may produce a better answer when given more time to work, while parameter count misses the extra inference computation.

r002.rationale: It does not propose translating a pretraining compute budget into the size of a conventional transformer trainable at a comparable token count.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss Jonas Geiping’s training node setup or whether it could train a 32-billion-parameter transformer.
